q: What makes a self-cleaning glass capable of repelling dirt and water effectively?
n: Most self-cleaning glass, such as Pilkington Activ, has a titanium-dioxide coating that is photocatalytic and hydrophilic. Sunlight breaks down organic dirt, and rain then sheets evenly across the glass and rinses it away instead of beading. Source: Pilkington technical literature; GANA Glazing Manual (Self-Cleaning Coatings).

q: A composite glass with one or more interlayers.
n: Laminated glass is two or more glass plies bonded with one or more plastic interlayers (PVB, SGP or EVA). If broken, the pieces stay adhered. Source: ASTM C1172 (Laminated Architectural Flat Glass); GANA Laminated Glazing Reference Manual.

q: What is the function of a low-e glass?
o: Reduces heat transfer while allowing light transmission
n: Low-E glass has a thin coating that reflects long-wave infrared (heat). It cuts heat transfer while still transmitting most visible light. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Low-Emissivity Coatings); ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals, Ch. 15 (Fenestration).

q: Placement of the glass into frames.
n: Glazing is the setting of glass into window or door frames with stops, beads, gaskets or compound. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Glazing); GANA Glazing Manual.

q: Slab thickness is critical in a project. What can be introduced to decrease the thickness of a suspended slab?
n: Drop panels thicken the slab locally around the columns. They resist punching shear and negative moment there, so the rest of a flat slab can be thinner. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 408 (Two-Way Slabs – Drop Panels); MacGregor & Wight, Reinforced Concrete.

q: In a high-rise building, what type of elevator system is typically preferred to minimize energy consumption and enhance ride comfort during long vertical travel?
n: High-rise buildings use traction elevators with counterweights. The counterweight balances the car, so less motor energy is needed, and gearless traction drives give smooth rides at high speed over long travel. Hydraulic and pneumatic lifts suit only low rises. Source: Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook; ASME A17.1.

q: Which component of an elevator system primarily controls the smooth acceleration and deceleration of the elevator car during operation?
n: A variable frequency drive varies the motor's frequency and voltage. That ramps speed smoothly, giving gentle acceleration and deceleration and accurate leveling. The governor is only a safety device for overspeed. Source: Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook; IEC 61800 (Adjustable Speed Drives).

q: In a traction elevator system, what is the primary function of the counterweight?
o: guide the elevator car during movement
balance the car load to reduce motor power requirements
prevent overspeed by regulating car speed
absorb shock at the bottom of the shaft
n: The counterweight balances the car plus about 40–50% of rated load. The motor then lifts only the out-of-balance load, which cuts the required power. Source: Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook; Stein & Reynolds, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings.

q: Which component of an escalator is primarily responsible for maintaining the tension and alignment of the moving steps during operation?
n: The step chains link the steps and run on sprockets. Kept under tension, they hold the steps in alignment along the truss. Source: EN 115-1 / ASME A17.1 (Escalators); Strakosch, The Vertical Transportation Handbook.

q: In an escalator system, which component is primarily responsible for guiding the movement of the handrail along its path?
n: The handrail runs on handrail guide rails (profiles) along the balustrade, which keep it on its path. A separate handrail drive moves it. Source: EN 115-1 / ASME A17.1 (Escalators – Handrail System).

q: What is the known tradename of conduit bodies?
n: "Condulet" is the long-established trade name (originally Crouse-Hinds) for conduit bodies such as LB, LL, LR, T and C fittings. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 3.14 (Conduit Bodies); Crouse-Hinds product history.

q: What type of switch is commonly used in machinery to detect the presence or absence of an object and automatically stop movement when a predetermined position is reached?
n: A limit switch is actuated by the moving part itself when it reaches a set position. It then stops or reverses the motion. Proximity switches sense objects without contact but are not end-of-travel stops. Source: NEMA ICS 5 (Control-Circuit and Pilot Devices); IEC 60947-5-1.

q: What is a sudden increase in voltage that can damage electrical equipment, typically caused by lightning strikes, power outages or the switching of heavy loads?
n: A surge (transient overvoltage) is a sudden voltage spike from lightning, utility switching or heavy loads cycling. It can damage electronics. Surge protective devices limit it. Source: IEEE C62.41 (Surge Environment); PEC Part 1, Art. 2.85 (Surge-Protective Devices).

q: What is the process of regulating and filtering incoming electrical power to ensure stable voltage and frequency, protecting sensitive equipment from spikes and surges?
n: Power conditioning regulates and filters the incoming supply so equipment gets stable voltage and frequency, free of spikes, surges, sags and noise. Source: IEEE Std 1100 (Powering and Grounding Electronic Equipment – Emerald Book).

q: What opens and closes a circuit?
n: A switch manually opens and closes a circuit. Fuses and breakers open automatically on faults, and relays are electrically operated switches. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 1.1 (Definitions – Switch) and Art. 4.4.

q: A brickwork or masonry bond composed of overlapping stretchers.
n: Running (stretcher) bond is all stretchers, each course overlapping the one below by half a unit. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5 (Masonry Bonds); Brick Industry Association Tech Note 30.

q: A brickwork or masonry bond having successive courses of stretchers with all head joints aligned vertically.
n: Stack bond lays stretchers with all head joints aligned vertically, so the units do not overlap. It needs joint reinforcement. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5; BIA Technical Note 30.

q: A brickwork bond having alternating headers and stretchers in each course, each header being centered above and below a stretcher.
n: Flemish bond alternates headers and stretchers within each course, with every header centered over the stretcher below. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5; BIA Technical Note 30.

q: A brickwork bond having a course of headers between every five or six courses of stretchers.
n: Common (American) bond has a course of headers every fifth or sixth course, with stretchers between. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5; BIA Technical Note 30.

q: A brickwork bond having alternate courses of headers and stretchers, in which the headers are centered on the stretchers and the joints between stretchers line up vertically in all courses.
n: English bond alternates whole courses of headers and stretchers, with headers centered on stretchers and stretcher joints aligned vertically. In English cross bond, alternate stretcher courses are shifted instead. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5; BIA Technical Note 30.

q: Which of the following components allows a window to be operable?
n: A sash becomes operable through its hardware for movement, such as hinges for casement and awning windows. Muntins divide the glass, glazing beads hold it, and a sash lock only secures the sash shut. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Windows).

q: To improve the seal and reduce drafts around a window, a flexible material was added to the edges where the window meets the frame. What is this addition called?
n: Weatherstripping is flexible strip material fitted where a sash meets its frame. It seals against air drafts, rain and dust. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Weatherstripping); ASTM E283 (Air Leakage).

q: In the MasterFormat classification system, which number division is designated for Doors and Windows?
n: CSI MasterFormat puts Openings (doors, windows, frames, hardware and glazing) in Division 08. Source: CSI/CSC MasterFormat (Division 08 – Openings).

q: To prevent a sliding barn door from swinging outward or wobbling during operation, which component is typically installed at the base of the door?
n: A floor guide (bottom guide) at the base of a sliding barn door rides in a slot or along the door's bottom edge. It keeps the door from swinging outward or wobbling. Source: Sliding door hardware manufacturers' installation guides; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8.

q: An H-handle is installed in what type of door?
n: H-type pull handles are mounted through frameless tempered glass doors, back to back on both faces. Source: Glass door hardware references; ANSI/BHMA A156.6 (Architectural Door Trim).

q: Continuous unobstructed slots for permitting movement due to changes in temperature or moisture.
n: Expansion joints are continuous unobstructed gaps through a structure or slab. They let parts expand and contract with temperature or moisture without damage. Source: ACI 224.3R (Joints in Concrete Construction); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Used as a plane of weakness in concrete.
n: Control (contraction) joints are sawn or tooled grooves that make a deliberate plane of weakness. Shrinkage cracking then occurs there instead of at random. Source: ACI 224.3R; ACI 302.1R.

q: A joint between fixed and moving segment.
n: An isolation joint fully separates elements that move differently, such as a slab and a column or wall. They then do not restrain each other. Source: ACI 224.3R (Isolation Joints); ACI 302.1R.

q: In construction, which of the following materials is not ideal for use as an expansion joint filler?
n: Expansion-joint fillers must be compressible and resilient: closed-cell foam, rubberized asphalt, bituminous fiberboard. Epoxy grout cures rigid and would block movement. Source: ACI 504R (Guide to Sealing Joints); ASTM D1751 / D1752.

q: Which of the following characteristics is most important for a good vapor retarder in building construction?
n: A vapor retarder must have low permeance (in perms), so it resists the diffusion of water vapor into the assembly. High permeance would let vapor pass. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals, Ch. 26 (Vapor Retarders); ASTM E96.

q: Which of the following is not ideal for use in structural concrete applications?
n: Lean concrete has a low cement content and low strength. It is used for blinding, mass fill and sub-base, not for structural members. Source: Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA); Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is the minimum concrete cover for cast-in-place footing?
n: Concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth, as in footings, needs at least 75 mm of cover over the reinforcement. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1 (Specified Concrete Cover – cast against and permanently in contact with ground); ACI 318.

q: What is the minimum concrete cover to protect stirrups and ties?
n: Cast-in-place beams and columns not exposed to weather or earth need 40 mm of cover over the primary bars, ties, stirrups and spirals. Source: NSCP 2015, Table 420.6.1.3.1; ACI 318.

q: Which type of rebar is used in slabs?
n: Trimmer bars are added around openings in slabs. They replace the cut bars and control cracking at the corners. Shear bars, ties and hoops belong to beams and columns. Source: ACI 315 (Details and Detailing of Concrete Reinforcement); CRSI Manual of Standard Practice.

q: What is the primary purpose of shear studs in reinforced concrete beams?
o: enhance composite action between steel and concrete
provide lateral confinement to longitudinal bars
act as a thermal expansion joint
increase the tensile strength of the concrete
n: Shear studs welded to the top flange of a steel beam anchor the concrete slab. They transfer horizontal shear, so steel and concrete act compositely. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 509 (Composite Members); AISC 360, Chapter I.

q: What type of foundation consists of a large, thick concrete slab that covers the entire footprint of a building, distributing the load evenly over a large area, especially suitable for soils with low bearing capacity?
n: A mat (raft) foundation is one thick slab under the whole building footprint. It spreads the load over soil of low bearing capacity and reduces differential settlement. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering (Mat Foundations); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 3.

q: What is the primary use of a sand blaster gun in construction and maintenance work?
n: Sandblasting propels abrasive at high speed to clean surfaces. It strips rust, mill scale, old paint and laitance before coating or repair. Source: SSPC-SP 5/SP 10 (Abrasive Blast Cleaning); ICRI 310.2R.
